original_value: This paper presents a new method for learning typed entailment graphs from text. We extract predicate-argument structures from multiple-source news corpora, and compute local distributional similarity scores to learn entailments between predicates with typed arguments (e.g., person contracted disease). Previous work has used transitivity constraints to improve local decisions, but these constraints are intractable on large graphs. We instead propose a scalable method that learns globally consistent similarity scores based on new soft constraints that consider both the structures across typed entailment graphs and inside each graph. Learning takes only a few hours to run over 100K predicates and our results show large improvements over local similarity scores on two entailment data sets. We further show improvements over paraphrases and entailments from the Paraphrase Database, and prior state-of-the-art entailment graphs. We show that the entailment graphs improve performance in a downstream task.

result.paraphrase: This paper introduces a new approach to learning typed entailment graphs from text. Predicate-argument structures are extracted from multi-source news corpora, and local distributional similarity scores are computed to learn entailments between predicates with typed arguments, such as person contracted disease. Earlier work relied on transitivity constraints to refine local decisions, but those constraints are computationally intractable on large graphs. We instead present a scalable method that learns globally consistent similarity scores using new soft constraints that account for both the structure across typed entailment graphs and the structure within each graph. Training runs in only a few hours over 100K predicates, and our results demonstrate substantial gains over local similarity scores on two entailment data sets. We also show improvements over paraphrases and entailments from the Paraphrase Database, as well as prior state-of-the-art entailment graphs. The entailment graphs further improve performance on a downstream task.
